name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_STATEMENT3_Q01 - Fundamental nature of periodic and oscillatory motions

questiontext.text:
Given below are three statements regarding periodic motion:

Statement I: Every oscillatory motion is necessarily periodic in nature.

Statement II: Every periodic motion is necessarily oscillatory in nature.

Statement III: In linear simple harmonic motion, the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement from the mean position and directed toward that mean position.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

periodic motion के संदर्भ में नीचे तीन कथन दिए गए हैं:

कथन I: प्रत्येक दोलनी गति अनिवार्य रूप से प्रकृति में आवर्ती होती है।

कथन II: प्रत्येक आवर्ती गति अनिवार्य रूप से प्रकृति में दोलनी होती है।

कथन III: रैखिक सरल आवर्त गति में, प्रत्यानयन बल माध्य स्थिति से विस्थापन के सीधे समानुपाती होता है और सदैव माध्य स्थिति की ओर निर्देशित होता है।

नीचे दिए गए विकल्पों में से सही उत्तर चुनें:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the first proposition regarding periodic motion:
Oscillatory motion is a to-and-fro movement about a fixed equilibrium position that repeats at regular time intervals, so all oscillatory motions are periodic.

Step 2: Evaluation of the second proposition regarding periodic motion:
Periodic motion merely repeats itself after a fixed time period without requiring an equilibrium point or a to-and-fro path. For example, uniform circular motion and planetary orbits are periodic but not oscillatory.

Step 3: Evaluation of the third proposition regarding periodic motion:
By Hooke's law for linear SHM, the restoring force satisfies \(F = -kx\), which is linearly proportional to displacement and opposite in direction (directed towards the equilibrium origin).

Final Answer: Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.

चरण 1: periodic motion से संबंधित प्रथम कथन का मूल्यांकन:
दोलनी गति एक निश्चित साम्यावस्था के परितः आगे-पीछे होने वाली गति है जो नियमित समयांतरालों में स्वयं को दोहराती है, अतः सभी दोलनी गतियाँ आवर्ती होती हैं।

चरण 2: periodic motion से संबंधित द्वितीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
आवर्ती गति केवल एक निश्चित समयांतराल बाद स्वयं को दोहराती है, इसमें किसी साम्यावस्था या आगे-पीछे गति की आवश्यकता नहीं होती। उदाहरणार्थ, एकसमान वृत्तीय गति और ग्रहों की कक्षाएँ आवर्ती हैं परंतु दोलनी नहीं हैं।

चरण 3: periodic motion से संबंधित तृतीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
रैखिक SHM के लिए हुक के नियम अनुसार, प्रत्यानयन बल \(F = -kx\) का पालन करता है, जो विस्थापन के समानुपाती और विपरीत दिशा में (माध्य स्थिति की ओर) होता है।

अंतिम उत्तर: कथन I और III सही हैं, लेकिन कथन II गलत है।

answer.text: Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_STATEMENT3_Q02 - Energy relations and time-averages in SHM

questiontext.text:
Given below are three statements regarding energy in shm:

Statement I: The total mechanical energy of an undamped linear simple harmonic oscillator is directly proportional to the square of its amplitude.

Statement II: During one complete cycle of simple harmonic motion, the kinetic energy of the oscillating particle attains its maximum value twice.

Statement III: The time-average of kinetic energy over a complete oscillation period is equal to the time-average of potential energy, with both averaging to \(\frac{1}{4}kA^2\).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

energy in shm के संदर्भ में नीचे तीन कथन दिए गए हैं:

कथन I: अवमंदन-रहित रैखिक सरल आवर्त दोलक की कुल यांत्रिक ऊर्जा उसके आयाम के वर्ग के सीधे समानुपाती होती है।

कथन II: सरल आवर्त गति के एक पूर्ण चक्र के दौरान, दोलन करते कण की गतिज ऊर्जा दो बार अपने अधिकतम मान को प्राप्त करती है।

कथन III: एक पूर्ण दोलन काल में गतिज ऊर्जा का समय-औसत मान स्थितिज ऊर्जा के समय-औसत मान के बराबर होता है, और दोनों का मान \(\frac{1}{4}kA^2\) होता है।

नीचे दिए गए विकल्पों में से सही उत्तर चुनें:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the first proposition regarding energy in shm:
The total mechanical energy is given by \(E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\). Since the spring constant \(k\) is constant for a given oscillator, the total energy is strictly proportional to \(A^2\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the second proposition regarding energy in shm:
In each oscillation period \(T\), the particle passes through the equilibrium position twice (once in each direction), where speed and kinetic energy reach their maximum values \(K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\).

Step 3: Evaluation of the third proposition regarding energy in shm:
The average value of \(\sin^2(\omega t)\) and \(\cos^2(\omega t)\) over a full cycle is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Thus, \(\langle K \rangle = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \langle\sin^2\rangle = \frac{1}{4}kA^2\) and \(\langle U \rangle = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \langle\cos^2\rangle = \frac{1}{4}kA^2\).

Final Answer: Statements I, II and III are all correct.

चरण 1: energy in shm से संबंधित प्रथम कथन का मूल्यांकन:
कुल यांत्रिक ऊर्जा \(E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\) होती है। दिए गए दोलक के लिए बल नियतांक \(k\) स्थिर होने से कुल ऊर्जा सीधे \(A^2\) के समानुपाती होती है।

चरण 2: energy in shm से संबंधित द्वितीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
प्रत्येक दोलन काल \(T\) में, कण साम्यावस्था से दो बार गुजरता है (दोनों दिशाओं में एक-एक बार), जहाँ चाल तथा गतिज ऊर्जा अपने अधिकतम मान \(K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2\) को प्राप्त करती हैं।

चरण 3: energy in shm से संबंधित तृतीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
एक पूर्ण चक्र में \(\sin^2(\omega t)\) तथा \(\cos^2(\omega t)\) का औसत मान \(\frac{1}{2}\) होता है। अतः \(\langle K \rangle = \frac{1}{4}kA^2\) और \(\langle U \rangle = \frac{1}{4}kA^2\) दोनों बराबर होते हैं।

अंतिम उत्तर: कथन I, II और III सभी सही हैं।

answer.text: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.
Statements I, II and III are all correct.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is correct, but Statements II and III are incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_STATEMENT3_Q03 - Kinematic phase relationships and acceleration in SHM

questiontext.text:
Given below are three statements regarding velocity and acceleration:

Statement I: In simple harmonic motion, the velocity of the oscillating particle leads its displacement by a phase angle of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) radians.

Statement II: At the mean position where the velocity of the particle reaches its maximum magnitude, the acceleration of the particle is zero.

Statement III: The velocity vector and the acceleration vector of a particle executing simple harmonic motion always point in the same direction throughout the motion.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

velocity and acceleration के संदर्भ में नीचे तीन कथन दिए गए हैं:

कथन I: सरल आवर्त गति में, दोलन करते कण का वेग उसके विस्थापन से \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) रेडियन की कला कोण से आगे (अग्रगामी) होता है।

कथन II: माध्य स्थिति पर, जहाँ कण का वेग अपने अधिकतम परिमाण पर पहुँचता है, कण का त्वरण शून्य होता है।

कथन III: सरल आवर्त गति कर रहे कण के वेग सदिश और त्वरण सदिश पूरी गति के दौरान सदैव एक ही दिशा में निर्देशित होते हैं।

नीचे दिए गए विकल्पों में से सही उत्तर चुनें:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the first proposition regarding velocity and acceleration:
Differentiating displacement \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega t)\) gives velocity \(v(t) = -\omega A\sin(\omega t) = \omega A\cos\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), showing a phase lead of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) radians.

Step 2: Evaluation of the second proposition regarding velocity and acceleration:
Acceleration is \(a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t)\). At the mean position (\(x = 0\)), the acceleration vanishes (\(a = 0\)), while velocity reaches its maximum magnitude \(v = \omega A\).

Step 3: Evaluation of the third proposition regarding velocity and acceleration:
When the particle moves away from the mean position toward an extreme, velocity points away from the center while acceleration points back toward the center (opposite directions). They point in the same direction only when moving toward the center.

Final Answer: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.

चरण 1: velocity and acceleration से संबंधित प्रथम कथन का मूल्यांकन:
विस्थापन \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega t)\) का अवकलन करने पर वेग \(v(t) = \omega A\cos\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) मिलता है, जो दर्शाता है कि वेग \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) रेडियन अग्रगामी है।

चरण 2: velocity and acceleration से संबंधित द्वितीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
त्वरण \(a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t)\) होता है। माध्य स्थिति (\(x = 0\)) पर त्वरण शून्य (\(a = 0\)) हो जाता है, जबकि वेग का परिमाण अधिकतम (\(\omega A\)) होता है।

चरण 3: velocity and acceleration से संबंधित तृतीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
जब कण माध्य स्थिति से चरम स्थिति की ओर गति करता है, तो वेग केंद्र से दूर तथा त्वरण केंद्र की ओर निर्देशित होता है (परस्पर विपरीत दिशा)। वे केवल केंद्र की ओर आते समय ही समान दिशा में होते हैं।

अंतिम उत्तर: कथन I और II सही हैं, लेकिन कथन III गलत है।

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_STATEMENT3_Q04 - Pendulum behavior in accelerating and orbital frames

questiontext.text:
Given below are three statements regarding the simple pendulum:

Statement I: A simple pendulum of length \(L\) mounted inside an automobile accelerating horizontally with constant acceleration \(a\) has a time period of \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{\sqrt{g^2 + a^2}}}\).

Statement II: Inside an artificial satellite in a circular orbit around Earth, a simple pendulum does not oscillate and its time period becomes infinitely large.

Statement III: When a simple pendulum swings with a large angular amplitude such as \(60^\circ\), its time period of oscillation is strictly equal to \(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

the simple pendulum के संदर्भ में नीचे तीन कथन दिए गए हैं:

कथन I: एकसमान क्षैतिज त्वरण \(a\) से गतिमान वाहन के अंदर लगे \(L\) लंबाई के सरल लोलक का आवर्तकाल \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{\sqrt{g^2 + a^2}}}\) होता है।

कथन II: पृथ्वी के चारों ओर वृत्तीय कक्षा में घूमते कृत्रिम उपग्रह के अंदर सरल लोलक दोलन नहीं करता है और उसका आवर्तकाल अनंत हो जाता है।

कथन III: जब कोई सरल लोलक \(60^\circ\) जैसे बड़े कोणीय आयाम के साथ दोलन करता है, तो उसका दोलन काल पूर्णतः \(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\) के बराबर होता है।

नीचे दिए गए विकल्पों में से सही उत्तर चुनें:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the first proposition regarding the simple pendulum:
In the horizontally accelerating frame, the effective gravitational acceleration is the vector resultant of gravity and the fictitious inertial acceleration: \(g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a^2}\). The period is \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the second proposition regarding the simple pendulum:
In the orbiting satellite, the frame is in free fall where the inward gravitational pull is exactly balanced by the outward centrifugal pseudo-force, making \(g_{\text{eff}} = 0\). With no restoring torque, the bob cannot oscillate, meaning \(T \to \infty\).

Step 3: Evaluation of the third proposition regarding the simple pendulum:
The formula \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\) is valid only in the small-angle approximation (\(\sin\theta \approx \theta\)). For large angles like \(60^\circ\), the exact restoring torque is smaller, and the true period \(T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\left(1 + \frac{\theta_0^2}{16}\right)\) is measurably longer.

Final Answer: Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.

चरण 1: the simple pendulum से संबंधित प्रथम कथन का मूल्यांकन:
क्षैतिज त्वरित निर्देश तंत्र में प्रभावी गुरुत्वीय त्वरण गुरुत्व और छद्म त्वरण का परिणामी होता है: \(g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a^2}\)। आवर्तकाल \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}}\) होता है।

चरण 2: the simple pendulum से संबंधित द्वितीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
कक्षा में घूमते उपग्रह में मुक्त पतन की स्थिति के कारण नेट प्रभावी गुरुत्व शून्य (\(g_{\text{eff}} = 0\)) हो जाता है। बिना प्रत्यानयन बल आघूर्ण के लोलक दोलन नहीं कर सकता, अतः \(T \to \infty\) होता है।

चरण 3: the simple pendulum से संबंधित तृतीय कथन का मूल्यांकन:
सूत्र \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\) केवल सूक्ष्म कोण सन्निकटन (\(\sin\theta \approx \theta\)) के लिए मान्य है। \(60^\circ\) जैसे बड़े आयाम के लिए प्रत्यानयन बल आघूर्ण कम होता है तथा वास्तविक आवर्तकाल \(2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\) से बड़ा होता है।

अंतिम उत्तर: कथन I और II सही हैं, लेकिन कथन III गलत है।

answer.text: Statements I, II and III are all correct.
Statements I and III are correct, but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is correct, but Statements II and III are incorrect.
Statements I and II are correct, but Statement III is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Matching physical parameters of simple harmonic motion

questiontext.text:
Match the physical parameters of a particle of mass \(m\) executing linear simple harmonic motion with amplitude \(A\) and angular frequency \(\omega\) (where \(k = m\omega^2\) is the force constant) given in List I with their corresponding mathematical expressions in List II:

List I List II
(A) Velocity amplitude (I) \(\omega^2 A\)
(B) Acceleration amplitude (II) \(\omega A\)
(C) Total mechanical energy (III) \(\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\)
(D) Angular frequency (IV) \(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A particle of mass \(m\) undergoes linear simple harmonic motion along the \(x\)-axis with amplitude \(A\), angular frequency \(\omega\), and spring/force constant \(k\). The position at time \(t\) can be represented as \(x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi)\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion occurs on a frictionless surface about the origin \(x = 0\) as the equilibrium mean position. The restoring force obeys Hooke's law, \(F = -kx\), and total mechanical energy is conserved.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Instantaneous velocity: \(v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\omega A \sin(\omega t + \phi)\)
- Instantaneous acceleration: \(a(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\omega^2 A \cos(\omega t + \phi) = -\omega^2 x(t)\)
- Total mechanical energy: \(E = K + U = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{2} k A^2\)
- Angular frequency from Newton's second law: \(m a = -k x \implies m(-\omega^2 x) = -k x \implies \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working and Evaluation
- Velocity amplitude represents the maximum magnitude of velocity: \(v_{\text{max}} = \omega A\).
- Acceleration amplitude represents the maximum magnitude of acceleration: \(a_{\text{max}} = \omega^2 A\).
- Total mechanical energy is constant at all times and equal to \(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\).
- Angular frequency in terms of spring constant and mass is \(\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All expressions have consistent physical dimensions: velocity amplitude is in \(\text{m s}^{-1}\), acceleration amplitude is in \(\text{m s}^{-2}\), total energy is in joules (\(\text{J}\)), and angular frequency is in \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\).
Therefore, the correct matching is: Velocity amplitude pairs with \(\omega A\); Acceleration amplitude pairs with \(\omega^2 A\); Total mechanical energy pairs with \(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\); Angular frequency pairs with \(\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Energy distribution at different positions in oscillations

questiontext.text:
A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion of amplitude \(A\) and total mechanical energy \(E\). Match the displacement positions given in List I with the corresponding energy characteristics given in List II:

List I (Displacement \(x\)) List II (Energy Characteristics)
(A) \(x = 0\) (I) Kinetic energy equals potential energy (\(K = U = \frac{E}{2}\))
(B) \(x = \pm A\) (II) Potential energy is zero and kinetic energy is maximum (\(U = 0\), \(K = E\))
(C) \(x = \pm \frac{A}{2}\) (III) Kinetic energy is zero and potential energy is maximum (\(K = 0\), \(U = E\))
(D) \(x = \pm \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\) (IV) Kinetic energy is three times the potential energy (\(K = 3U\))

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A simple harmonic oscillator has amplitude \(A\), force constant \(k\), and total mechanical energy \(E = \frac{1}{2} k A^2\). At displacement \(x\), the potential energy is \(U(x)\) and the kinetic energy is \(K(x)\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The equilibrium position is chosen at \(x = 0\) where potential energy \(U = 0\). Friction and other dissipative forces are neglected so that the total mechanical energy \(E = K + U\) remains constant throughout the motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Potential energy as a function of displacement: \(U(x) = \frac{1}{2} k x^2\)
- Kinetic energy as a function of displacement: \(K(x) = E - U(x) = \frac{1}{2} k (A^2 - x^2)\)
- Total energy: \(E = \frac{1}{2} k A^2\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working and Evaluation
- For displacement \(x = 0\) (mean position):
\(U = \frac{1}{2} k (0)^2 = 0\)
\(K = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 = E\)
Hence, potential energy is zero and kinetic energy is maximum (\(U = 0\), \(K = E\)).
- For displacement \(x = \pm A\) (extreme positions):
\(U = \frac{1}{2} k (\pm A)^2 = \frac{1}{2} k A^2 = E\)
\(K = E - U = 0\)
Hence, kinetic energy is zero and potential energy is maximum (\(K = 0\), \(U = E\)).
- For displacement \(x = \pm \frac{A}{2}\):
\(U = \frac{1}{2} k \left(\frac{A}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} \left(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\right) = \frac{E}{4}\)
\(K = E - U = E - \frac{E}{4} = \frac{3E}{4}\)
Taking the ratio: \(\frac{K}{U} = \frac{3E/4}{E/4} = 3 \implies K = 3U\).
Hence, kinetic energy is three times the potential energy.
- For displacement \(x = \pm \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\):
\(U = \frac{1}{2} k \left(\frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\right) = \frac{E}{2}\)
\(K = E - U = E - \frac{E}{2} = \frac{E}{2}\)
Hence, kinetic energy equals potential energy (\(K = U = \frac{E}{2}\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At every position, \(K + U = E\), confirming energy conservation. The calculated values correctly correlate with each physical state.
Therefore, the correct matching is: \(x = 0\) pairs with \(U = 0, K = E\); \(x = \pm A\) pairs with \(K = 0, U = E\); \(x = \pm \frac{A}{2}\) pairs with \(K = 3U\); \(x = \pm \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\) pairs with \(K = U = \frac{E}{2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Classification and periods of oscillatory time functions

questiontext.text:
Match the functions of time given in List I (where \(\omega\) is a positive constant) with their motion classification and fundamental time period given in List II:

List I (Function of time) List II (Classification and Time Period)
(A) \(f(t) = \sin \omega t - \cos \omega t\) (I) Periodic motion with time period \(\frac{\pi}{\omega}\)
(B) \(f(t) = \sin^2 \omega t\) (II) Periodic motion with time period \(\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\), but not simple harmonic
(C) \(f(t) = \cos \omega t + \cos 2\omega t\) (III) Simple harmonic motion with time period \(\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\)
(D) \(f(t) = e^{-\omega t}\) (IV) Non-periodic motion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four functions of time \(f(t)\) are provided, where \(\omega\) is a positive real constant representing angular frequency.

Step 2: Assumptions and Definitions
- A motion is periodic if \(f(t + T) = f(t)\) for the smallest non-zero positive constant \(T\) (the fundamental period).
- A periodic motion is simple harmonic if the displacement can be expressed in the single sinusoidal form \(f(t) = D \sin(\Omega t + \phi)\) or \(f(t) = D \cos(\Omega t + \phi)\) about an equilibrium point.
- If a function does not repeat its values after regular intervals, it is non-periodic.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Linear combination of harmonic terms of same frequency: \(A \sin \omega t + B \cos \omega t = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2} \sin\left(\omega t + \tan^{-1}\frac{B}{A}\right)\)
- Trigonometric power reduction identity: \(\sin^2 \omega t = \frac{1 - \cos 2\omega t}{2}\)
- Period of a sum of harmonic terms: least common multiple of individual periods.
- Monotonic exponential decay: \(e^{-\omega t} \to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working and Evaluation
- For \(f(t) = \sin \omega t - \cos \omega t\):
Multiplying and dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\):
\(f(t) = \sqrt{2}\left(\sin \omega t \cos\frac{\pi}{4} - \cos \omega t \sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sqrt{2}\sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\).
This is a single sinusoidal function of time with angular frequency \(\omega\). Hence, it represents simple harmonic motion with fundamental period \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}\).
- For \(f(t) = \sin^2 \omega t\):
Using the trigonometric identity: \(f(t) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos(2\omega t)\).
The time-dependent oscillating term has angular frequency \(\Omega = 2\omega\). Its fundamental period is \(T = \frac{2\pi}{2\omega} = \frac{\pi}{\omega}\). The motion is periodic with period \(\frac{\pi}{\omega}\).
- For \(f(t) = \cos \omega t + \cos 2\omega t\):
The first term has period \(T_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}\), and the second term has period \(T_2 = \frac{2\pi}{2\omega} = \frac{\pi}{\omega}\). The smallest time interval after which both terms repeat simultaneously is the least common multiple of \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), which is \(\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\). Because it is a superposition of two distinct harmonic frequencies (\(\omega\) and \(2\omega\)), the displacement is not a single harmonic sine or cosine function; thus it is periodic with period \(\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\), but not simple harmonic.
- For \(f(t) = e^{-\omega t}\):
The function decreases monotonically with time and tends to zero as \(t \to \infty\). It never repeats its values, so it is a non-periodic motion.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The periods and classifications match the canonical criteria of harmonic analysis.
Therefore, the correct matching is: \(f(t) = \sin \omega t - \cos \omega t\) pairs with Simple harmonic motion with time period \(\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\); \(f(t) = \sin^2 \omega t\) pairs with Periodic motion with time period \(\frac{\pi}{\omega}\); \(f(t) = \cos \omega t + \cos 2\omega t\) pairs with Periodic motion with time period \(\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\), but not simple harmonic; \(f(t) = e^{-\omega t}\) pairs with Non-periodic motion.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Time periods of various mechanical oscillating systems

questiontext.text:
Match the oscillating mechanical systems described in List I with their correct time period expressions for small oscillations given in List II:

List I (Oscillating System) List II (Time Period \(T\))
(A) A block of mass \(m\) attached between two identical horizontal springs, each of force constant \(k\), connected to rigid supports on opposite sides (I) \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\)
(B) A block of mass \(m\) attached to a single horizontal spring of force constant \(k\) on a frictionless surface (II) \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{2k}}\)
(C) A simple pendulum of length \(L\) executing small-angle oscillations in a stationary laboratory (III) \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{\sqrt{g^2 + \frac{v^4}{R^2}}}}\)
(D) A simple pendulum of length \(L\) suspended inside a car moving with uniform speed \(v\) on a horizontal circular track of radius \(R\) (IV) \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four distinct oscillating configurations are specified:
- A mass \(m\) flanked symmetrically by two identical springs of constant \(k\).
- A mass \(m\) attached to a single spring of constant \(k\).
- A simple pendulum of length \(L\) in a stationary reference frame with gravitational acceleration \(g\).
- A simple pendulum of length \(L\) in a vehicle moving along a horizontal circular path of radius \(R\) at constant speed \(v\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All springs are massless and obey Hooke's law. Motion is assumed frictionless. The pendulum string is inextensible and massless, and angular displacement \(\theta\) is sufficiently small so that \(\sin \theta \approx \theta\). In the rotating car, the centripetal acceleration is horizontal and orthogonal to downward gravity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Time period of a mass-spring linear harmonic oscillator: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k_{\text{eff}}}}\)
- Net restoring force for parallel two-spring displacement: \(F = F_1 + F_2 = -kx - kx = -2kx \implies k_{\text{eff}} = 2k\)
- Time period of a simple pendulum under effective acceleration \(g_{\text{eff}}\): \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}}\)
- Vector sum for perpendicular accelerations: \(g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a_c^2}\), where centripetal acceleration \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{R}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working and Evaluation
- For the mass between two springs:
When displaced by distance \(x\) from equilibrium, the spring on one side is extended by \(x\), pulling with force \(-kx\); the spring on the other side is compressed by \(x\), pushing in the same restoring direction with force \(-kx\).
The net restoring force is \(F_{\text{net}} = -2kx\).
Comparing with \(F = -k_{\text{eff}}x\) gives \(k_{\text{eff}} = 2k\).
The period of oscillation is: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{2k}}\).
- For the mass attached to a single spring:
The restoring force is \(F = -kx\).
The period of oscillation is: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\).
- For the stationary simple pendulum:
The restoring torque about the support is \(\tau = -mg L \sin \theta \approx -mg L \theta\).
With moment of inertia \(I = mL^2\), angular acceleration is \(\alpha = -\frac{g}{L}\theta\).
The period of oscillation is: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\).
- For the simple pendulum in the car navigating a circular path:
The car undergoes centripetal acceleration \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{R}\) directed horizontally toward the track center.
In the non-inertial reference frame of the car, an outward horizontal inertial pseudo-acceleration of magnitude \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{R}\) acts on the bob.
Because the downward vertical acceleration \(g\) and the horizontal acceleration \(a_c\) are mutually perpendicular, the effective acceleration due to gravity is:
\(g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a_c^2} = \sqrt{g^2 + \left(\frac{v^2}{R}\right)^2} = \sqrt{g^2 + \frac{v^4}{R^2}}\).
The period for small oscillations about this new equilibrium direction is: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{\sqrt{g^2 + \frac{v^4}{R^2}}}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
In each case, the dimensions evaluate correctly to time in seconds (\([T] = \text{s}\)). If \(v = 0\), the circular car expression reduces smoothly to the stationary pendulum result \(2\pi \sqrt{L/g}\).
Therefore, the correct matching is: Block between two identical springs pairs with \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{2k}}\); Block attached to a single spring pairs with \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}\); Simple pendulum in a stationary laboratory pairs with \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\); Simple pendulum in a car moving on a circular track pairs with \(2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{\sqrt{g^2 + \frac{v^4}{R^2}}}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q01 - Frequency and period of human heartbeats

questiontext.text: A human heart is observed to beat \(75\) times in \(1\text{ minute}\). What are the frequency and time period of the heartbeat?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of heartbeats: \(N = 75\)
Time duration: \(t = 1 ext{ minute} = 60 ext{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The heartbeats occur at regular, uniform time intervals, representing periodic motion.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Frequency: \( u = rac{N}{t}\)
Time period: \(T = rac{1}{ u}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate frequency:
\[ u = rac{75}{60 ext{ s}} = 1.25 ext{ s}^{-1} = 1.25 ext{ Hz}\]
Calculate time period:
\[T = rac{1}{1.25 ext{ s}^{-1}} = 0.8 ext{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check: \( u imes T = 1.25 imes 0.8 = 1.0\). Frequency is \(1.25 ext{ Hz}\) and time period is \(0.8 ext{ s}\).

Final Answer: \( u = 1.25 ext{ Hz}\), \(T = 0.8 ext{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q02 - Frequency of quartz crystal vibrations

questiontext.text: The period of vibration of a quartz crystal in an electronic watch is \(2.0\ \mu\text{s}\) (\(2.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}\)). What is the frequency of its vibrations in megahertz (\(\text{MHz}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Time period: \(T = 2.0\ \mu ext{s} = 2.0 imes 10^{-6} ext{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The vibrations are strictly periodic.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Frequency: \( u = rac{1}{T}\)
\(1 ext{ MHz} = 10^6 ext{ Hz}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ u = rac{1}{2.0 imes 10^{-6} ext{ s}} = 0.5 imes 10^6 ext{ Hz} = 0.5 ext{ MHz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\( u imes T = (0.5 imes 10^6) imes (2.0 imes 10^{-6}) = 1.0\). The frequency is \(0.5 ext{ MHz}\).

Final Answer: \(0.5 ext{ MHz}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q03 - Ratio of orbital period of comet to planet

questiontext.text: The orbital period of planet Mercury is \(88\text{ days}\) and Halley's comet appears every \(76\text{ years}\). Taking \(1\text{ year} = 365.25\text{ days}\), what is the ratio of the orbital period of Halley's comet to that of Mercury?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Period of Mercury: \(T_M = 88\text{ days}\)
Period of Halley's comet: \(T_H = 76\text{ years} = 76 \times 365.25\text{ days}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both orbits are periodic revolutions around the Sun.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Ratio: \(R = \frac{T_H}{T_M}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Total days for comet:
\[T_H = 76 \times 365.25 = 27759\text{ days}\]
Ratio calculation:
\[R = \frac{27759}{88} \approx 315.44 \approx 315\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(315 \times 88 = 27720 \approx 27759\). The ratio is approximately \(315\).

Final Answer: \(315\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q04 - Time period of periodic bouncing ball from height

questiontext.text: An ideal elastic ball is dropped from rest from a height of \(4.9\text{ m}\) above a horizontal floor and rebounds elastically to the same height. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the time period of this periodic motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Drop height: \(h = 4.9\text{ m}\)
Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)
Collision is perfectly elastic.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Air resistance is negligible. Downward motion takes time \(t_1\) and upward motion takes time \(t_2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Time to fall from rest: \(h = \frac{1}{2} g t_1^2 \implies t_1 = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}\)
For an elastic bounce, ascent time equals descent time: \(t_2 = t_1\)
Total time period: \(T = t_1 + t_2 = 2\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute values:
\[t_1 = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 4.9}{9.8}} = \sqrt{\frac{9.8}{9.8}} = \sqrt{1} = 1.0\text{ s}\]
Total period:
\[T = 2 \times 1.0\text{ s} = 2.0\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
One complete cycle consists of falling for \(1.0\text{ s}\) and rising for \(1.0\text{ s}\), giving a total period of \(2.0\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(2.0\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q05 - Time period of ball bouncing from elevated height

questiontext.text: A steel ball drops from a height of \(19.6\text{ m}\) onto a flat rigid plate and bounces elastically. Assuming no energy loss and taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the frequency of its periodic bouncing motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Height: \(h = 19.6\text{ m}\)
Gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Elastic collision means rebound speed equals impact speed. Motion is periodic under constant gravity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Descent time: \(t_{\text{down}} = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}\)
Period of cycle: \(T = 2 t_{\text{down}} = 2\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}\)
Frequency: \(\nu = \frac{1}{T}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate descent time:
\[t_{\text{down}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 19.6}{9.8}} = \sqrt{4} = 2.0\text{ s}\]
Period:
\[T = 2 \times 2.0\text{ s} = 4.0\text{ s}\]
Frequency:
\[\nu = \frac{1}{4.0\text{ s}} = 0.25\text{ Hz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The ball completes one full bounce cycle every \(4\text{ s}\), giving a frequency of \(0.25\text{ Hz}\).

Final Answer: \(0.25\text{ Hz}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q06 - Resultant amplitude of orthogonal harmonic components

questiontext.text: The displacement of a particle is given by \(x(t) = 3 \sin \omega t + 4 \cos \omega t\) (where \(x\) is in \(\text{cm}\)). What is the amplitude of the resulting simple harmonic motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Function: \(x(t) = A \sin \omega t + B \cos \omega t\)
Coefficients: \(A = 3\text{ cm}\), \(B = 4\text{ cm}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The two harmonic components have the same frequency \(\omega\) and are in phase quadrature.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Resultant amplitude: \(D = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[D = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ cm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\). The amplitude is \(5\text{ cm}\).

Final Answer: \(5\text{ cm}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q07 - Amplitude and maximum displacement calculation

questiontext.text: A particle executes SHM described by \(y(t) = 5 \cos \omega t + 12 \sin \omega t\) (in metres). What is the maximum displacement (amplitude) of the particle from the origin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Equation: \(y(t) = 5 \cos \omega t + 12 \sin \omega t\)
Coefficients: \(A = 5\text{ m}\), \(B = 12\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both components have the same angular frequency \(\omega\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Resultant amplitude: \(A_{\text{res}} = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[A_{\text{res}} = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Pythagorean triple \(5, 12, 13\). The maximum displacement is \(13\text{ m}\).

Final Answer: \(13\text{ m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q08 - Fundamental time period of combined sinusoidal waves

questiontext.text: A periodic function of time is given by \(f(t) = \sin(10\pi t) + \cos(20\pi t) + \sin(40\pi t)\) (in SI units). What is the fundamental time period of this motion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Angular frequencies: \(\omega_1 = 10\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\), \(\omega_2 = 20\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\), \(\omega_3 = 40\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The fundamental period \(T\) is the least common period of all three terms.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Individual periods: \(T_i = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_i}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(T_1 = \frac{2\pi}{10\pi} = 0.2\text{ s}\)
\(T_2 = \frac{2\pi}{20\pi} = 0.1\text{ s} = \frac{T_1}{2}\)
\(T_3 = \frac{2\pi}{40\pi} = 0.05\text{ s} = \frac{T_1}{4}\)
Since \(T_1\) is an integer multiple of \(T_2\) and \(T_3\), the smallest repeat interval is \(T = T_1 = 0.2\text{ s}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(t = 0.2\text{ s}\), all three terms complete integer cycles (1, 2, and 4 cycles). The fundamental period is \(0.2\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(0.2\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q09 - Time period of squared sine harmonic function

questiontext.text: What is the time period of the periodic function \(f(t) = \sin^2(50\pi t)\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Function: \(f(t) = \sin^2(50\pi t)\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Use trigonometric identity to write as a linear harmonic term.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\sin^2 \theta = \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}\)
Here \(\theta = 50\pi t\), so \(2\theta = 100\pi t\).
Effective angular frequency: \(\omega' = 100\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Period: \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega'}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[T = \frac{2\pi}{100\pi} = \frac{1}{50}\text{ s} = 0.02\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(\sin^2(50\pi(t + 0.02)) = \sin^2(50\pi t + \pi) = [-\sin(50\pi t)]^2 = \sin^2(50\pi t)\). The period is \(0.02\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(0.02\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q10 - Amplitude and phase of subtracted harmonic components

questiontext.text: A displacement function is given by \(x(t) = 6 \sin \omega t - 8 \cos \omega t\) (with \(x\) in \(\text{metres}\)). What are the amplitude \(A\) and initial phase \(\phi\) when expressed in standard cosine form \(x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi)\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(x(t) = 6 \sin \omega t - 8 \cos \omega t\)
Target: \(A \cos(\omega t + \phi) = A \cos \phi \cos \omega t - A \sin \phi \sin \omega t\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Amplitude \(A > 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Comparing coefficients:
\(A \cos \phi = -8\)
\(-A \sin \phi = 6 \implies A \sin \phi = -6\)
\(A = \sqrt{(-8)^2 + (-6)^2}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Amplitude:
\[A = \sqrt{64 + 36} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ m}\]
Phase angle:
\[\cos \phi = -0.8, \quad \sin \phi = -0.6\]
Since both sine and cosine are negative, \(\phi\) lies in the third quadrant:
\[\phi = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6}{8}\right) = \pi + \tan^{-1}(0.75)\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(10 \times (-0.8) = -8\) and \(-10 \times (-0.6) = +6\). The amplitude is \(10\text{ m}\).

Final Answer: \(A = 10\text{ m}\), \(\phi = \pi + \tan^{-1}(0.75)\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q11 - Time to travel from equilibrium to half amplitude

questiontext.text: A particle executes SHM with a time period \(T = 1.2\text{ s}\). What is the minimum time taken by the particle to travel from its mean position to a displacement equal to half of its amplitude (\(x = A/2\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Time period: \(T = 1.2\text{ s}\)
Start position: \(x = 0\) at \(t = 0\)
Final position: \(x = A/2\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Displacement from mean position: \(x(t) = A \sin \omega t\), where \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[A \sin \omega t = \frac{A}{2} \implies \sin \omega t = \frac{1}{2} \implies \omega t = \frac{\pi}{6}\]
\[t = \frac{\pi / 6}{2\pi / T} = \frac{T}{12}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[t = \frac{1.2\text{ s}}{12} = 0.1\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(t = 0.1\text{ s}\), \(\sin(2\pi \times 0.1 / 1.2) = \sin(\pi/6) = 0.5\). The time is \(0.1\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(0.1\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q12 - Time taken to travel between half and full amplitude

questiontext.text: A particle executes SHM with a time period \(T = 2.4\text{ s}\). What is the minimum time taken by the particle to travel from \(x = \frac{A}{2}\) to the extreme position \(x = A\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Time period: \(T = 2.4\text{ s}\)
Path: From \(x = A/2\) to \(x = A\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Motion starts from mean position \(x = 0\) at \(t = 0\): \(x(t) = A \sin \omega t\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Time from \(0\) to \(A/2\): \(t_1 = \frac{T}{12}\)
Time from \(0\) to \(A\): \(t_2 = \frac{T}{4}\)
Time from \(A/2\) to \(A\): \(\Delta t = t_2 - t_1 = \frac{T}{4} - \frac{T}{12} = \frac{T}{6}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\Delta t = \frac{T}{6} = \frac{2.4\text{ s}}{6} = 0.4\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The speed decreases towards the extreme position, so traveling the outer half of amplitude takes twice as long as the inner half: \(0.4\text{ s} = 2 \times 0.2\text{ s}\). The time is \(0.4\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(0.4\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q13 - Instantaneous displacement from harmonic motion equation

questiontext.text: A body oscillates with SHM according to the equation \(x = 5.0 \cos\left(2\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) (where \(x\) is in metres and \(t\) in seconds). What is the displacement of the body at \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\)? (Take \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(x(t) = 5.0 \cos\left(2\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\)
Time: \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Units are in the SI system.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Argument: \(\theta = 2\pi(1.5) + \frac{\pi}{4} = 3\pi + \frac{\pi}{4}\)
Reduction formula: \(\cos(3\pi + \alpha) = -\cos \alpha\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\cos\left(3\pi + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx -0.7071\]
\[x = 5.0 \times (-0.7071) = -3.5355\text{ m} \approx -3.54\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Displacement is bounded between \(-5.0\text{ m}\) and \(+5.0\text{ m}\). The displacement is approximately \(-3.54\text{ m}\).

Final Answer: \(-3.54\text{ m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q14 - Instantaneous acceleration calculation from displacement

questiontext.text: A body oscillates with SHM according to the equation \(x = 5.0 \cos\left(2\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) in SI units. What is the acceleration of the body at \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\)? (Take \(\pi^2 \approx 9.87\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Amplitude: \(A = 5.0\text{ m}\)
Angular frequency: \(\omega = 2\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Time: \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Acceleration in SHM satisfies \(a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t)\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Displacement at \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\):
\[x = 5.0 \cos\left(3\pi + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -5.0 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx -3.5355\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a = -\omega^2 x = -(2\pi)^2 \times (-3.5355) = 4\pi^2 \times 3.5355\]
With \(\pi^2 \approx 9.87\):
\[a \approx 4 \times 9.87 \times 3.5355 \approx 39.48 \times 3.5355 \approx +139.6\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx +140\text{ m s}^{-2}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since displacement is negative, the restoring acceleration must be positive. The acceleration is approximately \(+140\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Answer: \(+140\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q15 - Instantaneous speed calculation in SHM

questiontext.text: A body oscillates with SHM according to \(x = 5.0 \cos\left(2\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) in SI units. What is the speed of the body at \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\)? (Take \(\pi \approx 3.14\) and \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(x(t) = 5.0 \cos\left(2\pi t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\)
Time: \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Velocity: \(v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\omega A \sin\left(\omega t + \phi\right)\). Speed is the absolute magnitude \(|v(t)|\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\omega = 2\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\), \(A = 5.0\text{ m}\)
Argument at \(t = 1.5\text{ s}\): \(\theta = 3\pi + \frac{\pi}{4}\)
\(\sin\left(3\pi + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[v = -(2\pi \times 5.0) \times \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \frac{10\pi}{\sqrt{2}} = 5\pi\sqrt{2}\]
Substitute numerical values:
\[|v| \approx 5 \times 3.1416 \times 1.414 \approx 22.2\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 22\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Maximum possible speed is \(\omega A = 10\pi \approx 31.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). The calculated speed \(22\text{ m s}^{-1} < 31.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\) is physically consistent.

Final Answer: \(22\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q16 - Amplitude from maximum speed and acceleration

questiontext.text: A particle executing SHM has a maximum speed of \(16\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and a maximum acceleration of \(64\text{ m s}^{-2}\). What is the amplitude of oscillation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Maximum velocity: \(v_{\text{max}} = 16\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Maximum acceleration: \(a_{\text{max}} = 64\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Simple harmonic motion relationships: \(v_{\text{max}} = \omega A\) and \(a_{\text{max}} = \omega^2 A\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\omega = \frac{a_{\text{max}}}{v_{\text{max}}}\]
\[A = \frac{v_{\text{max}}}{\omega} = \frac{v_{\text{max}}^2}{a_{\text{max}}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[A = \frac{(16\text{ m s}^{-1})^2}{64\text{ m s}^{-2}} = \frac{256}{64} = 4\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(\omega = 64 / 16 = 4\text{ rad s}^{-1}\). Then \(v_{\text{max}} = 4 \times 4 = 16\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and \(a_{\text{max}} = 4^2 \times 4 = 64\text{ m s}^{-2}\). The amplitude is \(4\text{ m}\).

Final Answer: \(4\text{ m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q17 - Angular frequency from peak kinematic parameters

questiontext.text: A simple harmonic oscillator has a maximum speed of \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and a maximum acceleration of \(50\text{ m s}^{-2}\). What is its angular frequency \(\omega\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Maximum velocity: \(v_{\text{max}} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Maximum acceleration: \(a_{\text{max}} = 50\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard linear SHM relations.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(v_{\text{max}} = \omega A\)
\(a_{\text{max}} = \omega^2 A\)
\[\omega = \frac{a_{\text{max}}}{v_{\text{max}}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\omega = \frac{50\text{ m s}^{-2}}{10\text{ m s}^{-1}} = 5\text{ rad s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \(\text{s}^{-1}\) or \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\). The angular frequency is \(5\text{ rad s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer: \(5\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q18 - Speed calculation at intermediate displacement point

questiontext.text: A body executes SHM with an amplitude of \(0.10\text{ m}\) and a time period of \(2.0\text{ s}\). What is its speed when its displacement from the mean position is \(0.06\text{ m}\)? (Take \(\pi \approx 3.14\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Amplitude: \(A = 0.10\text{ m}\)
Time period: \(T = 2.0\text{ s}\)
Displacement: \(x = 0.06\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Displacement is measured from equilibrium.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Angular frequency: \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{2.0} = \pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Speed at displacement \(x\):
\[v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \sqrt{(0.10)^2 - (0.06)^2} = \sqrt{0.0100 - 0.0036} = \sqrt{0.0064} = 0.08\text{ m}\]
\[v = \pi \times 0.08\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 3.1416 \times 0.08 \approx 0.251\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(0.06, 0.08, 0.10\) forms a standard 3-4-5 proportional triangle. The speed is approximately \(0.251\text{ m s}^{-1}\) (or \(0.08\pi\text{ m s}^{-1}\)).

Final Answer: \(0.251\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q19 - Displacement corresponding to half maximum velocity

questiontext.text: A particle executes SHM with an amplitude \(A = 10\text{ cm}\). At what distance from the mean position is the speed of the particle equal to half of its maximum speed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Amplitude: \(A = 10\text{ cm}\)
Condition: \(v = \frac{1}{2} v_{\text{max}}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}\) and \(v_{\text{max}} = \omega A\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \frac{1}{2}\omega A \implies \sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \frac{A}{2}\]
\[A^2 - x^2 = \frac{A^2}{4} \implies x^2 = \frac{3A^2}{4} \implies |x| = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}A\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(A = 10\text{ cm}\):
\[|x| = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 10\text{ cm} = 5\sqrt{3}\text{ cm} \approx 5 \times 1.732 = 8.66\text{ cm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(8.66\text{ cm} < 10\text{ cm}\). The distance from the mean position is approximately \(8.66\text{ cm}\) (\(5\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\)).

Final Answer: \(8.66\text{ cm}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q20 - Acceleration magnitude calculation from displacement

questiontext.text: A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion at an angular frequency \(\omega = 5\text{ rad s}^{-1}\). What is the magnitude of its acceleration when its displacement from the mean position is \(4\text{ cm}\) (\(0.04\text{ m}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Angular frequency: \(\omega = 5\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Displacement: \(x = 0.04\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Magnitude of acceleration in linear SHM is \(|a| = \omega^2 |x|\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[|a| = \omega^2 |x|\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[|a| = (5\text{ rad s}^{-1})^2 \times 0.04\text{ m} = 25 \times 0.04 = 1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). The magnitude of the acceleration is \(1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Answer: \(1.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q21 - Oscillation frequency of horizontal mass-spring system

questiontext.text: A spring with spring constant \(k = 1200\text{ N m}^{-1}\) is attached to a mass \(m = 3\text{ kg}\) on a frictionless horizontal table. What is the frequency of oscillation \(\nu\) of the system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Spring constant: \(k = 1200\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Mass: \(m = 3\text{ kg}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Frictionless surface; ideal spring.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Angular frequency: \(\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\)
Frequency: \(\nu = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\omega = \sqrt{\frac{1200}{3}} = \sqrt{400} = 20\text{ rad s}^{-1}\]
\[\nu = \frac{20}{2\pi} = \frac{10}{\pi}\text{ Hz} \approx 3.18\text{ Hz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Time period is \(T = \frac{\pi}{10}\text{ s} \approx 0.314\text{ s}\). The frequency is \(\frac{10}{\pi}\text{ Hz}\).

Final Answer: \(\frac{10}{\pi}\text{ Hz}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q22 - Maximum acceleration of released spring-mass block

questiontext.text: A block of mass \(3\text{ kg}\) attached to a spring of force constant \(1200\text{ N m}^{-1}\) on a horizontal frictionless surface is pulled sideways by \(2.0\text{ cm}\) and released. What is the maximum acceleration of the block?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass: \(m = 3\text{ kg}\)
Spring constant: \(k = 1200\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Amplitude: \(A = 2.0\text{ cm} = 0.02\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Maximum acceleration occurs at the extreme displacement positions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\omega^2 = \frac{k}{m}\)
Maximum acceleration: \(a_{\text{max}} = \omega^2 A = \frac{k}{m} A\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a_{\text{max}} = \left(\frac{1200\text{ N m}^{-1}}{3\text{ kg}}\right) \times 0.02\text{ m} = 400 \times 0.02 = 8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Maximum restoring force is \(F_{\text{max}} = kA = 1200 \times 0.02 = 24\text{ N}\). Acceleration is \(F_{\text{max}} / m = 24 / 3 = 8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Answer: \(8.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q23 - Maximum speed of released horizontal spring oscillator

questiontext.text: A block of mass \(3\text{ kg}\) on a frictionless horizontal table is attached to a spring of spring constant \(1200\text{ N m}^{-1}\). If the block is pulled to \(2.0\text{ cm}\) from its equilibrium position and released from rest, what is its maximum speed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass: \(m = 3\text{ kg}\)
Spring constant: \(k = 1200\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Amplitude: \(A = 2.0\text{ cm} = 0.02\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Conservation of mechanical energy; maximum speed occurs at the equilibrium position \(x = 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\]
\[v_{\text{max}} = \omega A\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\omega = \sqrt{\frac{1200}{3}} = 20\text{ rad s}^{-1}\]
\[v_{\text{max}} = 20\text{ rad s}^{-1} \times 0.02\text{ m} = 0.40\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Energy check: \(\frac{1}{2} k A^2 = \frac{1}{2}(1200)(0.02)^2 = 0.24\text{ J}\). Maximum kinetic energy: \(\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text{max}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}(3)(0.4)^2 = 0.24\text{ J}\). Values match. The maximum speed is \(0.40\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer: \(0.40\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q24 - Mass determination from spring balance oscillation frequency

questiontext.text: A spring balance scale extends by \(20\text{ cm}\) under a maximum load of \(50\text{ kg}\). A body suspended from this balance oscillates vertically with a period \(T = 0.6\text{ s}\). Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the mass of the suspended body? (Round to one decimal place)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Maximum load: \(M = 50\text{ kg}\)
Extension: \(l = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m}\)
Period: \(T = 0.6\text{ s}\)
Gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Spring obeys Hooke's law.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Spring stiffness: \(k = \frac{M g}{l}\)
Period of oscillation: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} \implies m = \frac{k T^2}{4\pi^2}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute \(k\):
\[k = \frac{50 \times 9.8\text{ N}}{0.20\text{ m}} = 2450\text{ N m}^{-1}\]
Compute mass \(m\):
\[m = \frac{2450 \times (0.6)^2}{4\pi^2} = \frac{2450 \times 0.36}{39.478} = \frac{882}{39.478} \approx 22.34\text{ kg}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Rounding to one decimal place gives \(22.3\text{ kg}\).

Final Answer: \(22.3\text{ kg}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q25 - Time period of block coupled to two opposite springs

questiontext.text: A mass \(m = 3\text{ kg}\) on a frictionless horizontal floor is connected between two fixed vertical walls by two identical horizontal springs, each having spring constant \(k = 600\text{ N m}^{-1}\). What is the time period of oscillation of the mass?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass: \(m = 3\text{ kg}\)
Individual spring constant: \(k = 600\text{ N m}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
When the mass is displaced by \(x\), one spring is extended by \(x\) and the other is compressed by \(x\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Both restoring forces act in the same direction toward the mean position:
\[F_{\text{net}} = -kx - kx = -2kx\]
Effective spring constant: \(k_{\text{eff}} = 2k = 2 \times 600 = 1200\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Period: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k_{\text{eff}}}}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{3\text{ kg}}{1200\text{ N m}^{-1}}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{1}{400}} = 2\pi \times \frac{1}{20} = \frac{\pi}{10}\text{ s} \approx 0.314\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The effective stiffness is doubled, reducing the period by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\) compared to a single spring. The time period is \(\frac{\pi}{10}\text{ s}\) (\(\approx 0.314\text{ s}\)).

Final Answer: \(\frac{\pi}{10}\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q26 - Piston maximum velocity from stroke and angular frequency

questiontext.text: The stroke (twice the amplitude) of the piston in a locomotive cylinder is \(1.0\text{ m}\). If the piston moves with simple harmonic motion at an angular frequency of \(200\text{ rad min}^{-1}\), what is its maximum speed in \(\text{m s}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Stroke: \(2A = 1.0\text{ m} \implies A = 0.5\text{ m}\)
Angular frequency: \(\omega = 200\text{ rad min}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Convert angular frequency from \(\text{rad min}^{-1}\) to \(\text{rad s}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\omega = \frac{200\text{ rad}}{60\text{ s}} = \frac{10}{3}\text{ rad s}^{-1}\]
Maximum speed: \(v_{\text{max}} = \omega A\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[v_{\text{max}} = \left(\frac{10}{3}\text{ rad s}^{-1}\right) \times 0.5\text{ m} = \frac{5}{3}\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 1.67\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are \(\text{m s}^{-1}\). The maximum speed is \(\frac{5}{3}\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer: \(\frac{5}{3}\text{ m s}^{-1}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q27 - Total mechanical energy of linear harmonic oscillator

questiontext.text: A block of mass \(1\text{ kg}\) is attached to a spring of force constant \(k = 50\text{ N m}^{-1}\) on a frictionless horizontal table. If the block is pulled to a distance \(x = 10\text{ cm}\) from equilibrium and released from rest, what is the total mechanical energy of the system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass: \(m = 1\text{ kg}\)
Spring constant: \(k = 50\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Amplitude: \(A = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
No friction or dissipative forces; mechanical energy is conserved.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total energy in SHM: \(E = \frac{1}{2} k A^2\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E = \frac{1}{2} \times 50\text{ N m}^{-1} \times (0.10\text{ m})^2 = 25 \times 0.01 = 0.25\text{ J}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units are joules (\(\text{J}\)). Total energy is \(0.25\text{ J}\).

Final Answer: \(0.25\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q28 - Potential energy evaluation at specific displacement

questiontext.text: A block of mass \(1\text{ kg}\) fastened to a horizontal spring of spring constant \(k = 50\text{ N m}^{-1}\) oscillates with amplitude \(10\text{ cm}\). What is its potential energy when its displacement from the mean position is \(5\text{ cm}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Spring constant: \(k = 50\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Displacement: \(x = 5\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Potential energy is zero at the equilibrium position \(x = 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Potential energy: \(U = \frac{1}{2} k x^2\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[U = \frac{1}{2} \times 50\text{ N m}^{-1} \times (0.05\text{ m})^2 = 25 \times 0.0025 = 0.0625\text{ J}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(x = A/2\), \(U = \frac{1}{4} E_{\text{total}} = 0.25 / 4 = 0.0625\text{ J}\). The potential energy is \(0.0625\text{ J}\).

Final Answer: \(0.0625\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q29 - Kinetic energy calculation at intermediate position

questiontext.text: A block of mass \(1\text{ kg}\) on a spring of spring constant \(k = 50\text{ N m}^{-1}\) oscillates on a frictionless surface with amplitude \(10\text{ cm}\). What is its kinetic energy when it is \(5\text{ cm}\) away from the equilibrium position?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Spring constant: \(k = 50\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Amplitude: \(A = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\)
Displacement: \(x = 5\text{ cm} = 0.05\text{ m}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Total mechanical energy is conserved: \(E = K + U\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[E = \frac{1}{2} k A^2\]
\[K = E - U = \frac{1}{2} k (A^2 - x^2)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Total energy: \(E = \frac{1}{2}(50)(0.1)^2 = 0.25\text{ J}\)
Potential energy: \(U = \frac{1}{2}(50)(0.05)^2 = 0.0625\text{ J}\)
Kinetic energy:
\[K = 0.25\text{ J} - 0.0625\text{ J} = 0.1875\text{ J}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(K + U = 0.1875 + 0.0625 = 0.25\text{ J}\). Kinetic energy is \(0.1875\text{ J}\).

Final Answer: \(0.1875\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q30 - Kinetic energy percentage at half amplitude displacement

questiontext.text: A simple harmonic oscillator has a total mechanical energy of \(100\text{ J}\) and amplitude \(A\). What is its kinetic energy when its displacement from the mean position is \(x = \frac{A}{2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total energy: \(E = 100\text{ J}\)
Displacement: \(x = \frac{A}{2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Potential energy is zero at equilibrium.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(U = \frac{1}{2} k x^2\)
\(E = \frac{1}{2} k A^2\)
\(U = \frac{1}{2} k \left(\frac{A}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} \left(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\right) = \frac{1}{4} E\)
Kinetic energy: \(K = E - U = \frac{3}{4} E\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[K = \frac{3}{4} \times 100\text{ J} = 75\text{ J}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(x = A/2\), potential energy is \(25\text{ J}\) and kinetic energy is \(75\text{ J}\), summing to \(100\text{ J}\). The kinetic energy is \(75\text{ J}\).

Final Answer: \(75\text{ J}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q31 - Position of energy equipartition for given amplitude

questiontext.text: A harmonic oscillator has an amplitude \(A = 14.14\text{ cm}\). At what displacement from the mean position is its kinetic energy equal to its potential energy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Amplitude: \(A = 14.14\text{ cm} \approx 10\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\)
Condition: \(K = U\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Total energy \(E = K + U = 2U\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[U = \frac{1}{2} E \implies \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2} k A^2\right)\]
\[x^2 = \frac{A^2}{2} \implies |x| = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[|x| = \frac{14.14\text{ cm}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{14.14}{1.414} = 10.0\text{ cm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At \(x = 10\text{ cm}\), \(U = \frac{1}{2} k (100)\) and \(K = \frac{1}{2} k (200 - 100) = \frac{1}{2} k (100)\), so \(K = U\). The displacement is \(\pm 10.0\text{ cm}\).

Final Answer: \(\pm 10.0\text{ cm}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q32 - Precise length calculation of Earth seconds pendulum

questiontext.text: A simple pendulum ticks seconds (completes each half-swing in \(1\text{ s}\), so \(T = 2.0\text{ s}\)). If \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(\pi^2 = 9.87\), what is the length of this pendulum to two decimal places?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Time period: \(T = 2.0\text{ s}\)
Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)
Constant: \(\pi^2 = 9.87\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Small angular oscillations; ideal massless inextensible string.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \implies L = \frac{g T^2}{4\pi^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[L = \frac{9.8 \times (2.0)^2}{4 \times 9.87} = \frac{9.8 \times 4}{4 \times 9.87} = \frac{9.8}{9.87} \approx 0.9929\text{ m} \approx 0.99\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
A seconds pendulum has a length of approximately \(0.99\text{ m}\) (or \(1\text{ m}\)).

Final Answer: \(0.99\text{ m}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q33 - Time period calculation of pendulum on lunar surface

questiontext.text: A simple pendulum has a time period of \(3.5\text{ s}\) on the Earth's surface where \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\). What is its time period on the Moon where acceleration due to gravity is \(1.7\text{ m s}^{-2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Earth period: \(T_E = 3.5\text{ s}\)
\(g_E = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)
\(g_M = 1.7\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Pendulum length \(L\) is unchanged.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}} \implies \frac{T_M}{T_E} = \sqrt{\frac{g_E}{g_M}}\]
\[T_M = T_E \sqrt{\frac{g_E}{g_M}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\frac{g_E}{g_M} = \frac{9.8}{1.7} \approx 5.7647\]
\[\sqrt{5.7647} \approx 2.401\]
\[T_M = 3.5\text{ s} \times 2.401 \approx 8.4\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Weaker gravity yields a longer period: \(8.4\text{ s} > 3.5\text{ s}\). The time period on the Moon is approximately \(8.4\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(8.4\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q34 - Effective acceleration and period in circular motion

questiontext.text: A car travels with uniform speed \(v = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}\) on a horizontal circular track of radius \(R = 40\text{ m}\). What is the effective acceleration \(g_{\text{eff}}\) experienced by a simple pendulum suspended inside the car? (Take \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and round to the nearest whole number)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Speed: \(v = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Radius: \(R = 40\text{ m}\)
Gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The car's frame is accelerated horizontally by centripetal acceleration \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{R}\). The vertical gravitational acceleration is downward.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Centripetal acceleration: \(a_c = \frac{v^2}{R}\)
Effective acceleration: \(g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a_c^2}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[a_c = \frac{(20)^2}{40} = \frac{400}{40} = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}\]
\[g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{(9.8)^2 + (10)^2} = \sqrt{96.04 + 100} = \sqrt{196.04} \approx 14.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\sqrt{196} = 14\), the effective acceleration is approximately \(14\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Answer: \(14\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q35 - Pendulum time period in vertically accelerating lift

questiontext.text: A simple pendulum of length \(L = 1.47\text{ m}\) is suspended in an elevator accelerating upward at \(a = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(\pi \approx 3.14\), what is the time period of oscillation for small swings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length: \(L = 1.47\text{ m}\)
Upward acceleration: \(a = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-2}\)
Gravity: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In an upward accelerating elevator, the pseudo-force acts downward.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Effective acceleration: \(g_{\text{eff}} = g + a\)
Time period: \(T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}}\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[g_{\text{eff}} = 9.8 + 4.9 = 14.7\text{ m s}^{-2}\]
\[\frac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}} = \frac{1.47\text{ m}}{14.7\text{ m s}^{-2}} = 0.10\text{ s}^2\]
\[T = 2\pi \sqrt{0.10} \approx 2 \times 3.1416 \times 0.3162 \approx 1.99\text{ s} \approx 2.0\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Increased effective gravity reduces the period from the static value \(2\pi\sqrt{1.47/9.8} = 2.43\text{ s}\) to \(2.0\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(2.0\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_MCQ_Q36 - Time period of symmetric dual mass-spring system

questiontext.text: A spring of spring constant \(k = 400\text{ N m}^{-1}\) has two equal masses of \(m = 2.0\text{ kg}\) attached at its two ends on a frictionless floor. If both masses are pulled outward by equal forces and released, what is the time period of oscillation of each mass?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Spring constant: \(k = 400\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Mass at each end: \(m = 2.0\text{ kg}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Center of mass of the system remains stationary. Symmetrical oscillation about the center.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Using reduced mass \(\mu = \frac{m \cdot m}{m + m} = \frac{m}{2} = 1.0\text{ kg}\):
\[T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{k}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{2k}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\mu = \frac{2.0}{2} = 1.0\text{ kg}\]
\[T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{1.0\text{ kg}}{400\text{ N m}^{-1}}} = 2\pi \times \frac{1}{20} = \frac{\pi}{10}\text{ s} \approx 0.314\text{ s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The period of a single mass on the full spring would be \(2\pi\sqrt{2/400} = \frac{\sqrt{2}\pi}{20} \approx 0.44\text{ s}\). For the two-mass system, \(T = \frac{\pi}{10}\text{ s} \approx 0.314\text{ s}\).

Final Answer: \(\frac{\pi}{10}\text{ s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Chronological order of events during SHM cycle

questiontext.text:
A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion along the x-axis with time period \(T\) about the mean position \(x = 0\). At time \(t = 0\), the particle is released from rest at the positive extreme position \(x = +A\).

Consider the following four events occurring during its first complete oscillation from \(t = 0\) to \(t = T\):

(I) Potential energy of the particle first reaches its maximum value after release.
(II) Kinetic energy of the particle first reaches its maximum value.
(III) The particle first returns to the positive extreme position.
(IV) Speed of the particle is maximum while it moves in the positive x-direction.

Arrange these events in the correct chronological order from earliest to latest:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The oscillating particle has amplitude \(A\), time period \(T\), and angular frequency \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}\). At \(t = 0\), the particle is released from rest at \(x(0) = +A\) with initial velocity \(v(0) = 0\). The interval under consideration is one full cycle, \(0 \le t \le T\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The motion is idealized with no damping forces. The origin \(x = 0\) is the mean (equilibrium) position. Motion towards the right is taken as positive displacement, and towards the left as negative displacement.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Displacement from the positive extreme is described by: \[x(t) = A\cos(\omega t)\] Velocity is given by: \[v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\omega A\sin(\omega t)\] Kinetic energy is \(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), which is maximum when speed is maximum (\(x = 0\)). Potential energy is \(U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2\), which is maximum at the extremes (\(|x| = A\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For kinetic energy to first reach its maximum, the particle must reach the mean position \(x = 0\). Setting \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega t) = 0\) yields the earliest positive phase \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\). Substituting \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}\) gives: \[t = \frac{\pi}{2\omega} = \frac{T}{4}\] 2. For potential energy to first reach its maximum after release, the particle must reach the opposite extreme \(x = -A\). Setting \(A\cos(\omega t) = -A\) yields \(\omega t = \pi\), giving: \[t = \frac{\pi}{\omega} = \frac{T}{2}\] 3. For speed to be maximum while traveling in the positive direction, velocity must equal \(+\omega A\). Setting \(v(t) = -\omega A\sin(\omega t) = +\omega A\) gives \(\sin(\omega t) = -1\). The earliest positive phase is \(\omega t = \frac{3\pi}{2}\), which gives: \[t = \frac{3\pi}{2\omega} = \frac{3T}{4}\] 4. For the particle to return to its initial starting point \(x = +A\), \(\cos(\omega t) = 1\), corresponding to completing one full oscillation at: \[\omega t = 2\pi \implies t = T\] Comparing the determined time values: \[\frac{T}{4} < \frac{T}{2} < \frac{3T}{4} < T\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The computed sequence of times monotonically increases over the interval from zero to \(T\). The chronological order is: kinetic energy first reaching maximum at a quarter period, followed by potential energy reaching maximum at the negative extreme at half period, followed by maximum speed in the positive direction at three-quarters of a period, and concluding with the particle returning to the release point at the full period.
Correct sequence: (II) → (I) → (IV) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Derivation steps for simple pendulum period

questiontext.text:
Consider the following four logical steps involved in the standard derivation of the time period of a simple pendulum of length \(L\) and bob mass \(m\) executing small oscillations:

(I) Apply the small-angle approximation \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) to express angular acceleration as \(\alpha = -\left(\frac{mgL}{I}\right)\theta\).
(II) Formulate the restoring torque acting on the bob about the support due to the tangential component of gravity as \(\tau = -mgL\sin\theta\).
(III) Substitute the moment of inertia \(I = mL^2\) and extract angular frequency \(\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}\) to obtain \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\).
(IV) Equate the restoring torque to \(I\alpha\) using Newton's rotational law to write \(I\alpha = -mgL\sin\theta\).

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of steps from beginning to conclusion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A simple pendulum consists of a point mass \(m\) suspended by a massless, inextensible string of length \(L\) from a rigid pivot, oscillating in a vertical plane with angular displacement \(\theta\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The string remains taut. Angular displacement \(\theta\) is measured from the vertical mean position. The restoring torque tends to decrease \(\theta\), introducing a negative sign.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Torque about pivot: \[\tau = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}_{\text{tangential}}\] Newton's second law for rotation: \[\tau = I\alpha\] Small angle series approximation for \(\theta \ll 1\text{ rad}\): \[\sin\theta \approx \theta\] Angular acceleration relation in angular SHM: \[\alpha = -\omega^2\theta \implies T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}\] Moment of inertia of a point mass at distance \(L\): \[I = mL^2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. First, gravity \(mg\) is resolved into components. The radial component \(mg\cos\theta\) is balanced by string tension minus centripetal requirement, while the tangential component \(mg\sin\theta\) acts perpendicular to the string. The torque about the support point is computed as lever arm times tangential force: \(\tau = -L(mg\sin\theta)\).
2. Second, using the rotational equation of motion \(\tau = I\alpha\), this torque is set equal to the product of moment of inertia and angular acceleration: \(I\alpha = -mgL\sin\theta\).
3. Third, for small amplitudes, \(\sin\theta\) is replaced by \(\theta\) in radians, giving the linear differential form \(\alpha = -\left(\frac{mgL}{I}\right)\theta\), which demonstrates harmonic motion.
4. Fourth, the moment of inertia for the bob \(I = mL^2\) is substituted into the expression, simplifying it to \(\alpha = -\left(\frac{g}{L}\right)\theta\). Identifying \(\omega^2 = \frac{g}{L}\) gives \(\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}\) and yields the time period \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The logical progression follows from force resolution to torque formulation, then applying dynamic equilibrium, linearizing via small-angle approximation, and finally evaluating geometric parameters to obtain the period.
Correct sequence: (II) → (IV) → (I) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Chronological sequence of kinematic and energy states

questiontext.text:
A particle performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude \(A\) and period \(T\). At time \(t = 0\), the particle passes through the mean position \(x = 0\) moving in the positive x-direction.

Consider the following four conditions and the earliest times at which they are satisfied:

(I) Kinetic energy of the particle becomes equal to its potential energy.
(II) Magnitude of acceleration of the particle reaches half of its maximum value.
(III) The particle passes the position \(x = \frac{A}{2}\) while returning towards the mean position.
(IV) Potential energy of the particle reaches its maximum value.

Arrange these conditions in chronological order of their first occurrence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The motion is simple harmonic with amplitude \(A\), time period \(T\), and angular frequency \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}\). At \(t = 0\), \(x(0) = 0\) and \(v(0) > 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Displacement is taken along the x-axis with \(x = 0\) at the center of oscillation. The initial displacement is zero and velocity is directed along \(+x\), so the displacement is represented by a sine function.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Displacement: \[x(t) = A\sin(\omega t)\] Velocity and acceleration: \[v(t) = \omega A\cos(\omega t), \quad a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t) = -\omega^2 A\sin(\omega t)\] Maximum acceleration magnitude: \[a_{\max} = \omega^2 A\] Kinetic and potential energies: \[K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(A^2 - x^2), \quad U = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. For magnitude of acceleration to reach half of maximum: \[|a(t)| = \frac{1}{2}a_{\max} \implies \omega^2 |x| = \frac{1}{2}\omega^2 A \implies |x| = \frac{A}{2}\] With \(x = A\sin(\omega t)\), the earliest positive time gives: \[\sin(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2} \implies \omega t = \frac{\pi}{6} \implies t = \frac{\pi}{6\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)} = \frac{T}{12} \approx 0.0833 T\] 2. For kinetic energy to equal potential energy: \[K = U \implies \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 \implies 2x^2 = A^2 \implies x = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}\] Substituting \(x = A\sin(\omega t)\): \[\sin(\omega t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \implies \omega t = \frac{\pi}{4} \implies t = \frac{\pi}{4\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)} = \frac{T}{8} = 0.125 T\] 3. For potential energy to reach maximum, the particle must reach the positive extreme \(x = +A\): \[\sin(\omega t) = 1 \implies \omega t = \frac{\pi}{2} \implies t = \frac{\pi}{2\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)} = \frac{T}{4} = 0.250 T\] 4. For the particle to pass \(x = \frac{A}{2}\) while returning towards the mean position, its velocity must be negative (\(\cos(\omega t) < 0\)): \[\sin(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2} \text{ with } \omega t \text{ in the second quadrant} \implies \omega t = \pi - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\] The corresponding time is: \[t = \frac{5\pi}{6\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)} = \frac{5T}{12} \approx 0.4167 T\] Comparing the times: \[\frac{T}{12} < \frac{T}{8} < \frac{T}{4} < \frac{5T}{12}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The time values satisfy \(0 < \frac{T}{12} < \frac{T}{8} < \frac{T}{4} < \frac{5T}{12} < \frac{T}{2}\). Therefore, the events occur in the order: acceleration magnitude reaching half-maximum, followed by kinetic energy equaling potential energy, then potential energy reaching maximum, and finally passing the half-amplitude position during the return journey.
Correct sequence: (II) → (I) → (IV) → (III).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_OSCILLATIONS_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Progression of dynamical states from extreme to mean

questiontext.text:
A block attached to an ideal horizontal spring executes simple harmonic motion of amplitude \(A\) and period \(T\) on a frictionless surface. At time \(t = 0\), the block is released from rest at the positive extreme position \(x = +A\).

As the block moves from \(x = +A\) towards the mean position \(x = 0\) during its first quarter cycle, consider the following four states:

(I) The kinetic energy of the block becomes equal to its potential energy.
(II) The magnitude of the restoring force drops to half of its maximum value.
(III) The potential energy of the block is three times its kinetic energy.
(IV) The acceleration of the block first becomes zero.

Arrange these states in the chronological order in which they are encountered by the block:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A mass-spring system oscillates with amplitude \(A\), spring constant \(k\), and period \(T\). The block is released from rest at \(t = 0\) from \(x = +A\). We trace the progression as displacement decreases from \(x = +A\) to \(x = 0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The surface is frictionless and the spring obeys Hooke's law, \(F = -kx\). The displacement is parameterized as \(x(t) = A\cos(\omega t)\), where \(\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}\).
